**The Moon Is Leaving**

Every year, the moon drifts about four centimeters farther from Earth—roughly the rate at which our fingernails grow. No one notices. No one could. But measured across deep time, the separation is real, and it's reshaping everything.

When the moon was young and close, it hung enormous in the sky, and Earth spun faster; days lasted perhaps four hours. The tides it raised dragged against the planet's rotation, and in an act of cosmic bookkeeping, Earth's lost spin became the moon's gained distance. We have been slowing down and pushing it away ever since—an exchange running for four billion years.

Eventually—long after anything human remains, after the last city crumbles and every word ever spoken scatters—the moon will look small in the sky, total solar eclipses will become impossible, and Earth's days will stretch toward weeks. The companionship is temporary. Everything's is.

There's something almost unbearable about this, and also something consoling. The moon isn't abandoning us dramatically; it's simply obeying physics, the same gentle arithmetic that governs every parting. Most losses work this way—not betrayal, just drift. A friend you stop calling. A hometown that changes while your back is turned. The slow accumulation of centimeters until you realize you're somewhere else entirely.

For now, though, it still rises. Still hauls the oceans across the shores twice a day. Still lights the way home for moths and lovers and insomniacs. Whole civilizations have lived and died beneath it, none the wiser.

The leaving has barely started.
